'''Annie Dookhan''' (born 1977) is an American chemist who was convicted of felony obstruction of justice, tampering with evidence, and other crimes relating to mass falsification of lab results. At the time of her crimes, she worked at the [[Massachusetts]] Department of Public Health Drug Abuse lab,<ref name="mass.gov sentenced"/> but was placed on administrative leave and subsequently quit after admitting to falsifying evidence affecting up to 34,000 cases.<ref name="npr">{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/2013/03/14/174269211/mass-crime-lab-scandal-reverberates-across-state|title=Crime Lab Scandal Leaves Mass. Legal System In Turmoil|website=Npr.org|access-date=24 September 2018}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Annie Dookhan was born Annie Sadiyya Khan into an [[Indo-Trinidadian]] family in [[San Fernando, Trinidad and Tobago|San Fernando]], [[Trinidad and Tobago]] in 1977.<ref name="bostonglobe lies">{{cite news|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2013/02/03/chasing-renown-path-paved-with-lies/Axw3AxwmD33lRwXatSvMCL/story.html|title=Annie Dookhan chased renown on a path paved with lies|newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]]|access-date=24 September 2018}}</ref> She moved to the United States when she was a child and eventually became a citizen.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/2012/10/15/for-mass-lab-chemist-unlikely-road-scandal/bv4bGE437pakb39WBIN2dP/story.html|title=For Mass. Lab chemist, an unlikely road to scandal - Boston.com|access-date=2013-12-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140102194024/http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/2012/10/15/for-mass-lab-chemist-unlikely-road-scandal/bv4bGE437pakb39WBIN2dP/story.html|archive-date=2014-01-02|url-status=dead }}</ref> 

Dookhan attended [[Regis College (Massachusetts)|Regis College]] for two years before earning a Bachelor of Science degree in biochemistry from the [[University of Massachusetts Boston]] in 2001. In 2010, a coworker found that Dookhan was claiming on her resume that she had earned a master's degree from the [[University of Massachusetts]].<ref name="MassLive-2012">{{Cite web |date=2012-10-13 |title=For Mass. lab chemist Annie Dookhan, an unlikely road to scandal |url=https://www.masslive.com/news/2012/10/for_mass_lab_chemist_annie_dookhan.html |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20240308023706/https://www.masslive.com/news/2012/10/for_mass_lab_chemist_annie_dookhan.html |archive-date=March 8, 2024 |access-date=2020-12-14 |work=[[MassLive]] |language=en |agency=The Associated Press}}</ref> During her time working at the Hinton State Laboratory Institute, Dookhan also claimed to be attending night classes as part of a PhD program at [[Harvard University]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Bruney|first=Gabrielle|date=2020-04-01|title=Annie Dookhan's Drug Lab Crimes Compromised More Than 20,000 Criminal Convictions|url=https://www.esquire.com/entertainment/tv/a31994111/annie-dookhan-now-how-to-fix-a-drug-scandal-netflix-true-story/|access-date=2020-12-14|website=Esquire|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Career==
In 2003, Dookhan was hired as a chemist at the Hinton State Laboratory Institute in the [[Jamaica Plain]] neighborhood of [[Boston]].<ref name="WBURTimeline">[http://badchemistry.wbur.org/timeline Timeline of case] from [[WBUR]] in Boston</ref>

===Evidence falsification===
In June 2011, an evidence officer at the lab discovered that Dookhan had tested 95 samples without properly signing them out. Further investigation revealed that she had forged the initials of an evidence officer in her log book, and she was suspended from lab duties.<ref name="statement of case">{{cite web|url=https://s3.amazonaws.com/s3.documentcloud.org/documents/563115/statement-of-the-case-dookhan.pdf|title=Statement of Case against Dookhan|website=S3.amazonaws.com|access-date=24 September 2018}}</ref> However, she was still allowed to continue testifying in court until February 2012, when district attorneys throughout the Boston area were notified of the breach in protocol and Dookhan was placed on administrative leave. She resigned in March 2012.<ref name=WBURTimeline/>

During Dookhan's time at the Hinton lab, it had been run by the Massachusetts Department of Health's Office of Human Services. However, in a cost-cutting move, the [[Massachusetts General Court]] transferred control of the lab to the [[Massachusetts State Police]] forensics unit in 2011. The state police mounted a probe into the Dookhan case.<ref name=WBURTimeline/> The probe revealed that Dookhan's superiors had ignored [[Red flag (idiom)|red flags]] surrounding her before 2011. For instance, she reportedly tested over 500 samples per month—five times the normal average—even though her supervisors and colleagues claimed to have never seen her in front of a microscope, and that she frequently misidentified samples.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.cbsnews.com/news/massachusetts-lab-tech-arrested-for-alleged-improper-handling-of-drug-tests|title=Massachusetts lab tech arrested for alleged improper handling of drug tests|last=Quijano|first=Elaine|authorlink=Elaine Quijano|work=[[CBS News]]|date=2012-09-29}}</ref> Additionally, Dookhan's productivity remained steady after the [[Supreme Court of the United States]] ruled in ''[[Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts]]'' that chemists who perform drug tests in criminal cases can be subpoenaed to testify in person. According to an independent data analysis by [[WBUR-FM|WBUR]], Dookhan's turnaround time for tests actually dropped from 2009 to 2011.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://badchemistry.wbur.org/2013/05/15/annie-dookhan-drug-testing-productivity|title=With More Work, Less Time, Dookhan's Tests Got Faster|last=Amico|first=Chris|publisher=[[WBUR]]|date=2013-05-15}}</ref> The problem was severe enough that [[Governor of Massachusetts|Governor]] [[Deval Patrick]] ordered the lab shut down.<ref>{{cite news|url= http://boston.cbslocal.com/2012/08/30/i-team-state-drug-testing-lab-closed-amid-concerns-of-mishandled-evidence|title=State Drug Lab Chemist's Actions Could Affect Thousands of Cases|last= Anderson|first= Karen|publisher= [[WBZ-TV]]|date= 2012-08-30}}</ref>

In August, police interviewed Dookhan at her home in [[Franklin, Massachusetts|Franklin]], where she admitted to altering and faking test results in order to cover up her frequent "dry labbing", or visually identifying samples without actually testing them. She even went as far as to add cocaine to samples in which no cocaine was present.<ref name="statement of case"/> She said she had been dry-labbing for as long as three years. At one point, she broke down, saying, "I messed up, I messed up bad. I don't want the lab to get in trouble."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://s3.documentcloud.org/documents/700555/dookhan-interviews-all.pdf|title=Interim Summary of Annie Dookhan|website=S3.documentcloud.org|access-date=3 December 2018}}</ref>

===Charges===
On September 28, 2012, Dookhan was arrested and charged with [[obstruction of justice]] and falsification of academic records. The latter charge came because she had claimed both on her resume and in sworn testimony to have had a master's degree in chemistry from the [[University of Massachusetts Boston]]. However, school officials revealed that Dookhan had no such degree, and had never taken master's level classes there.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.boston.com/metrodesk/2012/09/28/arrest-warrants-issued-for-chemist-heart-state-drug-lab-scandal/CWKCO8JdmvCf7WlrbY5pPK/story.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120929154447/http://www.boston.com/metrodesk/2012/09/28/arrest-warrants-issued-for-chemist-heart-state-drug-lab-scandal/CWKCO8JdmvCf7WlrbY5pPK/story.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 29, 2012|title=Bail set at $10,000 after arraignment of Annie Dookhan, chemist in state drug lab scandal|last=Arsenault|first=Mark|newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]]|date=2012-09-28}}</ref>

On December 17, Dookhan was formally arraigned on 27 charges—17 counts of obstruction of justice, eight counts of tampering with evidence and one count each of perjury and falsification of records. Prosecutors alleged that whenever a second test failed to confirm the initial results, Dookhan would tamper with the vials to make them consistent with the inaccurate results obtained by her dry labbing. She was also charged with falsely certifying results that she knew to be compromised; these certifications were admitted as evidence in court.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wbur.org/2012/12/17/drug-lab-charges|title=More Charges For Mass. Chemist In Drug Lab Scandal|website=www.wbur.org|date=17 December 2012 |access-date=24 September 2018}}</ref>

===Imprisonment===
On November 22, 2013, Dookhan was sentenced to three to five years of imprisonment and two years of probation by Judge Carol S. Ball in Suffolk Superior Court, after pleading guilty to crimes relating to falsifying drug tests.<ref name="mass.gov sentenced">{{cite web|url=http://www.mass.gov/ago/news-and-updates/press-releases/2013/2013-11-22-dookhan-plea.html|title=Annie Dookhan Pleads Guilty to Tampering with Evidence, Obstruction|date=22 November 2013|website=Mass.gov|access-date=24 September 2018}}</ref><ref name="ap sentenced">{{cite web|url=http://bigstory.ap.org/article/guilty-plea-expected-mass-drug-lab-scandal|title=Mass. Chemist pleads guilty in drug lab scandal|access-date=2013-12-04|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131230235708/http://bigstory.ap.org/article/guilty-plea-expected-mass-drug-lab-scandal|archive-date=2013-12-30 }}</ref><ref name="boston sentenced">{{cite web|url=https://www.boston.com/news/local-news/2013/11/22/annie-dookhan-former-state-chemist-who-mishandled-drug-evidence-sentenced-to-3-to-5-years-in-prison/|title=Annie Dookhan, former state chemist who mishandled drug evidence, sentenced to 3 to 5 years in prison|date=22 November 2013|website=Boston.com|access-date=24 September 2018}}</ref> This was greater than the one-year sentence her defense requested, but less than the five to seven-year sentence requested by the prosecution.<ref name="ap sentenced"/><ref name="boston sentenced"/> However, Ball said that upward departure was merited due to the ramifications of Dookhan's misconduct. Ball wrote, "Innocent persons were incarcerated, guilty persons have been released to further endanger the public, millions and millions of public dollars are being expended to deal with the chaos Ms. Dookhan created, and the integrity of the criminal justice system has been shaken to the core."<ref name="boston sentenced"/>

Dookhan, [[Massachusetts Department of Correction]] inmate F81328, served her sentence at [[Massachusetts Correctional Institution – Framingham]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.vinelink.com/vinelink/detailsAction.do?siteId=20000&agency=1&id=F81328&searchType=offender|title=Inmate information from Vinelink and Massachusetts Department of Correction|website=Vinelink.com|access-date=24 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131230234654/https://www.vinelink.com/vinelink/detailsAction.do?siteId=20000&agency=1&id=F81328&searchType=offender|archive-date=30 December 2013|url-status=dead|df=dmy-all}}</ref> By April 2016, she had been granted parole and was subsequently released from prison.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wbur.org/2016/04/12/annie-dookhan-paroled|title=Annie Dookhan, Chemist At Center Of Mass. Drug Lab Scandal, Is Out Of Prison|website=www.wbur.org|date=12 April 2016 |access-date=24 September 2018}}</ref><ref>[https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2016/04/12/annie-dookhan-key-figure-state-lab-scandal-released-from-prison/lp7q98UmWKucv4F7O3R4DI/story.html Annie Dookhan, key figure in state lab scandal, released from prison], Boston Globe, April 12, 2016</ref>

===Impact===
In January 2015, Benjamin Keehn, a prominent defense attorney with the Committee for Public Counsel Services, said that as many as 40,000 people could have been falsely convicted as a result of Dookhan's actions.<ref>[https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2015/01/09/thousands-drug-convictions-stake-dookhan-case/0EsGAC6f1nzVSEhRzdaVWN/story.html ACLU argues for drug-crime defendants in Annie Dookhan saga], Boston Globe, January 9, 2015</ref>

In May 2015, the [[Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court]] ruled that defendants whose convictions on drug charges were based on evidence potentially tainted by Dookhan could pursue retrials without having to face more charges or tougher sentences. However, they would need a retrial to be released.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Trager|first1=Rebecca|title=Thousands of U.S. Convicts Can Get New Trials Because of Rogue Drug Lab Chemist|url=http://www.scientificamerican.com/article/thousands-of-u-s-convicts-can-get-new-trials-because-of-rogue-drug-lab-chemist/|website=Scientific American|access-date=29 May 2015}}</ref>

On April 18, 2017, Massachusetts dropped more than 21,000 low-level drug criminal charges involving Dookhan. Out of the 15,570 cases in which she was involved, only 117 were to be pursued, according to Daniel Conley, the district attorney in Suffolk County, which includes Boston. Other counties followed suit, taking direction from the state Supreme Court to select a small fraction of cases for re-prosecution.<ref>[https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/epic-drug-lab-scandal-results-more-20-000-convictions-dropped-n747891 Drug Lab Scandal Results in More Than 20,000 Convictions Dropped], NBC News, April 18, 2017</ref>

Dookhan's story was the subject of a [[Netflix]] series, ''[[How to Fix a Drug Scandal]]'' created by [[Erin Lee Carr]] that was released April 1, 2020.<ref name=WBUR-DrugScandal-2020>{{cite news|last1=Trahan|first1=Erin|title=Netflix's 'How To Fix A Drug Scandal' Elevates Process Over Personality|url=https://www.wbur.org/artery/2020/04/09/netflix-how-to-fix-a-drug-scandal-review|work=WBUR|date=9 April 2020|language=en}}</ref> The four-part documentary focuses on Dookhan and an independent case of fraud in a different drug lab by Sonja Farak. ''How to Fix a Drug Scandal'' depicts the role of former [[Massachusetts Attorney General|Attorney General]] of [[Massachusetts]] [[Martha Coakley]], who was accused of political cover up.<ref name=Vox-DrugScandal-2020>{{cite news|last1=Wilkinson|first1=Alissa|title=How to Fix a Drug Scandal is the staggering true story of justice gone very wrong|url=https://www.vox.com/culture/2020/4/1/21200503/how-to-fix-a-drug-scandal-netflix-review-dookhan-farak|work=Vox|date=1 April 2020|language=en}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Dookhan married Surrendranath Dookhan, a software engineer, in 2004.<ref name="bostonglobe lies"/> They have one son, Branden Dookhan.<ref name="MassLive-2012" />
